response:
My take: **your return is not “hard” in the big picture, but it is complex enough that paying $350 for your first self-employment year is reasonable.** If I were you, I would probably **hire the CPA for this year** and then use **TurboTax Self-Employed next year** using her return as a template.

Here’s how I’d think about it.

## Your complexity level: low-to-moderate

You have:

- Regular W-2 income
- ~$15,000 side consulting income, probably 1099-NEC
- A new brokerage account
- Likely Schedule C / self-employment tax questions
- Maybe state/local complications

That is not a deeply complex tax return — no business entity, no inventory, no multiple states, no complex investments, no rental properties mentioned — but it is definitely more than a basic W-2 return.

The newest part for you is the **self-employment piece**. That usually means:

- Form 1040, Schedule C
- Self-employment tax on Schedule SE
- Possible business deductions
- Possibly estimated tax concerns going forward
- Clean separation of personal and business expenses

Those are not too bad if your records are organized, but they are the area where you are most likely to make a mistake or miss something because it is new.

## Why TurboTax Self-Employed could work

TurboTax Self-Employed is a legitimate choice for your situation, especially if:

- Your side gig is relatively simple
- You know exactly what you earned
- You know what business expenses you had
- You have bank statements, 1099s, invoices, and receipts
- You are comfortable going line by line through Schedule C
- You are okay not having a person ready for an audit or follow-up question

TurboTax will guide you through Schedule C and self-employment tax. It can absolutely handle a W-2 job plus 1099 consulting income.

The main catch: **it only knows what you tell it.**

It does not automatically “know” that you bought software, drove to client meetings, used home office space, paid for equipment, etc. You have to enter that information. It also will not make professional judgment calls about whether a deduction is ordinary and necessary, or whether a particular common expense should be deducted.

So TurboTax is fine if your records are clean and you are confident you can identify every business expense.

## Why the CPA might be worth the extra $230

The CPA quote is more than just “file my return.” She may also provide:

- A first-time self-employment return done correctly
- Review of your Schedule C categories
- Confirmation that self-employment tax was calculated properly
- State/local issue spotting
- Basic tax planning for next year
- A person to call if there are questions
- Audit support, at least initially

That last point matters because a DIY software program does not call you on the phone when the IRS asks for a follow-up. A CPA can also explain, in plain English, why certain deductions were taken or not taken.

For $350, especially if it includes both federal and state, I would not call that crazy for a first year with self-employment.

## The brokerage account part

If you only started contributing to a regular brokerage account, that may not add much to the return yet. A contribution by itself is not taxable income.

It becomes more relevant if you have:

- Interest or dividend income exceeding the threshold that requires reporting on Schedule B
- Capital gains from selling investments
- 1099-B, 1099-DIV, or 1099-INT forms
- Cryptocurrency or other digital asset questions
- Short-term capital gains
- Losses carried forward
- Wash sale issues

If none of that happened, the brokerage account is not the reason to pay a CPA. The freelance income is the bigger factor.

## My practical recommendation

I’d do one of these:

### Option 1: Best for peace of mind — Hire the CPA this year

Use the CPA for this year because this is your first year with self-employment income.

Then:

- Ask her to explain the main Schedule C items in simple terms.
- Ask which deductions were taken and why.
- Ask what I should track next year.
- Ask whether I need estimated tax payments.
- Save the return and ask if you can do it yourself next year.
- Possibly ask if she would do a discounted review next year if you file yourself.

This is probably the best balance of cost and safety.

### Option 2: Budget-focused — Use TurboTax Self-Employed

I would choose TurboTax if:

- Your $15,000 freelance income is mostly clear
- You have no messy expense tracking
- You know your business deductions are simple or nonexistent
- You had good withholding from your W-2 job
- You do not have complicated investment activity
- You are okay doing the self-employment parts carefully yourself

In that case, TurboTax Self-Employed is probably fine.

### Option 3: Hybrid — Prepare in TurboTax, then pay for a review

If the CPA will accept a prepared return for review, this could be a smart middle path.

You prepare the return in TurboTax Self-Employed, then pay her maybe $100–$250 to review it before filing. That gives you:

- Lower cost
- Professional check
- Less DIY risk
- A learning experience for next year

You would need to ask if she offers that, because some CPAs only quote a full prep price.

## Red flags that make me more likely to use the CPA

I would lean more strongly toward the CPA if any of these are true:

- You used a home office for a portion of your home
- You drove for business and are keeping mileage
- You bought business equipment, software, or supplies
- You may have had a net business loss
- You worked for multiple clients but are not sure how to report all income
- You have questions about how much to set aside for self-employment tax
- You are unsure whether some expenses are deductible
- You made estimated tax payments, or you think you should have
- You have both W-2 and 1099 income and are worried about withholding
- You want audit support or tax planning included

If you have a couple of those, the CPA starts to look pretty obviously worth it.

## Bottom line

Your situation is **not so complex that you must hire a CPA**, but it is **complex enough that paying $350 for your first self-employment year is defensible**.

If I were you, I would probably say: **use the CPA this year once, because self-employment is new and the cost difference is not life-changing. Then switch to TurboTax next year when you have a clean template and understand the basics.**

If budget is the main concern and your freelance records are very clean, TurboTax Self-Employed is a reasonable choice. Just be very careful with Schedule C and self-employment tax, and make sure you understand whether you need to adjust withholding or make estimated payments going forward.
